prompt: A ticket: after a meeting where the laptop was plugged into the room's television by HDMI, the user says the laptop's own speakers have gone silent. What do you check first?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 4.

choices.text: Whether the HDMI port on the laptop was damaged by the plug being pulled out at an angle
choices.why: A damaged video port would not silence the internal speakers; the sound was sent elsewhere.

choices.text: The audio driver, reinstalled from the maker's site
choices.why: Nothing is broken; a reinstall is an afternoon spent on a setting.

choices.text: The green jack on the side, for a loose headphone plug
choices.why: Plausible for silence in general, but the HDMI meeting is the change that explains it.

choices.text: The output device in the sound settings, which the system moved to the new screen when it appeared
choices.why: HDMI carries audio, and the system switched output to the television when it appeared.

prompt: A user has a new 4K monitor and says the computer has become slow: the pointer moves across the screen in visible steps, and everything else runs normally. What is the likely cause?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 4.

choices.text: The processor cannot draw four times as many pixels and has started throttling
choices.why: Throttling slows the work, not only the pointer, and it comes with heat.

choices.text: An old cable or port running the picture at 30 Hz
choices.why: HDMI 1.4 manages 4K only at 30 Hz, which works and looks like a slow machine.

choices.text: A mouse whose DPI is too low for the larger resolution
choices.why: DPI changes how far the pointer travels, not how smoothly the screen redraws it.

choices.text: Too little memory for a 4K desktop
choices.why: Running out of memory slows everything and grows with what is open.

prompt: A phone headset with a single plug is used on an office desktop. The user hears the call but nobody hears them, and no microphone setting changes that. What solves it?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 4.

choices.text: A splitter that turns the one plug into two
choices.why: The headset is TRRS; the desktop's two sockets are TRS, so the microphone wire is connected to nothing.

choices.text: Moving the plug from the green socket to the pink one
choices.why: Then the microphone might work and the sound would stop; one plug cannot sit in both.

choices.text: Raising the microphone gain until the other side can hear something
choices.why: There is no signal to amplify when the wire is not connected.

choices.text: Updating the sound card driver, since the headset is newer than the machine and the old driver does not know it
choices.why: A 3.5 mm jack needs no agreement between the ends; it is wiring, not software.

prompt: A laptop that wants 65 W is plugged into a USB-C phone charger. It charges while asleep and loses charge while the user works. What is happening?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 4.

choices.text: The battery is at the end of its life
choices.why: A worn battery holds less; it does not charge only while the machine sleeps.

choices.text: Its output in watts is below what the machine draws under load
choices.why: Power Delivery negotiates what the charger can give; a 20 W brick charges slowly or not at all under load.

choices.text: The USB-C socket on the laptop is loose and loses contact whenever the keyboard is being used
choices.why: A loose socket responds to the cable being moved, not to how hard the machine is working.

choices.text: The port has no DisplayPort Alternate Mode
choices.why: Alt Mode is about video over USB-C; charging is a separate negotiation.

prompt: At a small office, every browser says it cannot find any site. The router's settings page at `192.168.0.1` opens, the line light is green, and a page that answers on its number loads. Where is the fault?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 13.

choices.text: In the Wi-Fi, which is connected but too weak to carry pages
choices.why: A weak radio would slow the page by number too, and the settings page opened.

choices.text: In the line to the street, which the provider has to repair before anything will load again
choices.why: The line light is green and a page by number crossed it.

choices.text: In DHCP, which has run out of leases
choices.why: Machines with no address could not open the router's page.

choices.text: In name lookup: the step that turns a site's name into its address
choices.why: When DNS fails everything looks broken and nothing is; the address test separates the two.

prompt: After the office was closed for two weeks, the laptops can no longer find the network printer, which was set up by its number. What is the lasting fix the course recommends?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 13.

choices.text: Typing a fixed address into the printer's own menu
choices.why: It works until the router hands that number to someone else, because it does not know to avoid it.

choices.text: Reinstalling the printer driver on each laptop
choices.why: The laptops are looking at the old number; a new driver looks at it too.

choices.text: Moving the printer onto the guest network
choices.why: Devices on the guest network cannot reach anything else in the building.

choices.text: A reservation on the router so the printer always receives the same address
choices.why: Its lease lapsed and it came back with a new number; the reservation keeps the router informed.

prompt: A customer bought a better router and plugged it in behind the provider's box. The internet works, but the laptops cannot find the printer or each other. What does the lesson say to do?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 13.

choices.text: Put the provider's box into bridge mode
choices.why: Two devices both routing is the commonest cause of this; the provider's box should only convert.

choices.text: Return the new router, because a provider's modem will not work with anything else behind it
choices.why: Using your own router is supported; the box has a mode for exactly this.

choices.text: Give the two routers the same Wi-Fi name and password
choices.why: The radio settings are not the problem; both boxes are still routing.

choices.text: Hold the pinhole reset on the new router
choices.why: A reset restores defaults and leaves both boxes routing.

prompt: A workstation keeps freezing. You restart it in safe mode and it freezes there too. What does that result tell you?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 14.

choices.text: A startup program is the cause
choices.why: Startup programs do not run in safe mode, so they cannot be what froze it there.

choices.text: Uninstalling programs will not help; suspect the hardware or the system itself
choices.why: Safe mode removes what was added; a fault that survives it is not in what was added.

choices.text: The test was inconclusive, so the next step is to reinstall the drivers one at a time
choices.why: It was conclusive: the fault is below what safe mode strips away.

choices.text: It is a virus hiding from safe mode
choices.why: A guess reached for when structure runs out; the test has already placed the fault.

prompt: A user's synced folder now holds `budget.xlsx` and `budget (Ana's MacBook).xlsx`. She wants to keep the newer one and delete the other. What do you advise?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 11.

choices.text: Keep the newer one, because the service always names the losing copy after the device
choices.why: The name records where the copy came from, not which one holds the work.

choices.text: Delete both and restore from the bin
choices.why: The bin holds deleted files, not the version before the conflict.

choices.text: Open both, or run Compare, before deleting either
choices.why: The older copy was edited on the offline device and may hold work the newer one never had.

choices.text: Turn sync off on the MacBook so it stops happening
choices.why: That leaves one machine's work in one place, and does not settle which copy is right.

prompt: A user wants her Outlook `.pst` file inside her OneDrive folder so it is the same on the desktop and the laptop. What is the risk?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 11.

choices.text: It will count twice against her quota, once for each machine that holds it
choices.why: Quota counts what is stored in the account, once.

choices.text: Two machines writing to it risk leaving one corrupt copy
choices.why: It is one file holding a database; sync can produce corruption rather than two copies.

choices.text: The mail inside it becomes readable by anyone with the folder link
choices.why: A private folder is not shared by being synced.

choices.text: Two conflict copies, which she can compare
choices.why: That is the ordinary file case; a database file can be damaged instead.

prompt: A user deleted a shared file from Drive and uploaded a corrected one with the same name. Colleagues' links now say the file does not exist. What should she have done instead?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 11.

choices.text: Kept the original file and replaced its contents through Manage versions
choices.why: That keeps the identifier the links point at.

choices.text: Uploaded it into a different folder so the old path would not clash
choices.why: The link points at an identifier, not a path; a new upload is a new identifier wherever it goes.

choices.text: Renamed the new file so it differs from the deleted one by a letter
choices.why: The name was never what the link used.

choices.text: Emptied the bin first, so the old file stops blocking the name
choices.why: Nothing is blocking a name; the links still point at the deleted file's identifier.

prompt: Ransomware encrypted a user's documents. His backup drive, which lives plugged into the machine, turns out to be encrypted too. What does the course say would have saved it?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 8.

choices.text: Disconnecting it once each backup has finished, until the next one
choices.why: A drive that is always connected is part of the machine, and ransomware treats it as a folder.

choices.text: A faster drive, so the nightly copy finishes before the ransomware reaches it
choices.why: Speed does not change what a connected drive is exposed to.

choices.text: Mirroring the drive every hour instead of every night
choices.why: A mirror copies the damage, and more often means sooner.

choices.text: Encrypting the backup drive with the system's checkbox
choices.why: That protects a drive carried away, not one the infected machine can write to.

prompt: A customer pays for a 200-megabit line and complains that the file manager shows downloads at `25` megabytes per second. How many megabits per second is that download?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 13.

prompt: "The Wi-Fi is slow." The lesson's method: run the speed test on Wi-Fi in the room where it feels slow, then run it again on a ___ plugged into the router.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 13.

prompt: A user let a caller claiming to be support take remote control of her laptop. Put what she does next in the order the lesson gives.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 16.
items: Change the password, from her phone rather than that laptop
Sign out of every session
Check recovery details, forwarding rules and any added second factor
Call the bank on the number on the card
Change that password everywhere else it was used
trap: Signing out before changing the password lets the attacker sign straight back in with the one they already have.

prompt: Match each report from a user to the fault the lesson reads in it.
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 15.

pairs.left: Charges only while the cable is held at an angle
Lines across the picture that change as the lid moves
pairs.right: the ribbon cable through the hinge

pairs.left: Several neighbouring keys stopped at once
Crashes in different programs, with different messages

prompt: A small office asks which jobs its own staff can reasonably do without special tools. Which does the lesson put on the do-it-yourself side?
hint: Essential Computing, lesson 15.

choices.text: Swapping a memory module
choices.why: It unplugs, and a mistake costs the module.

choices.text: Cleaning out dust
choices.why: A can of compressed air and ten minutes.

choices.text: Replacing a desktop's disk
choices.why: It is a part that unplugs.

choices.text: Renewing the thermal paste
choices.why: The heatsink comes off and both surfaces are cleaned; that is a job to take somewhere.

choices.text: Replacing a laptop screen
choices.why: A ribbon cable in the lid is where a mistake costs the lid.

choices.text: Replacing a power supply
choices.why: The lesson lists it among the jobs to take somewhere.

prompt: A laptop on the office network shows the address `169.254.12.40` and reaches nothing. What does that address tell you?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4.

choices.text: It was given an address from a different private range, used by larger offices
choices.why: The private ranges are 10, 172.16 and 192.168; 169.254 is what a machine picks when nobody answers.

choices.text: Its DNS server is not answering, so names fail
choices.why: A DNS fault leaves a normal address in place and breaks only names.

choices.text: Its lease was renewed with a new public address
choices.why: A lease hands out the network's own addresses; this one came from no server.

choices.text: Nobody answered its DHCP request
choices.why: It gave itself a link-local address; look at the cable, the Wi-Fi association or the server.

prompt: Since Monday, about half the office's machines cannot reach the internet, with no pattern by floor or by model, and each one's settings look correct. Somebody mentions a new box by the coffee machine. What fits?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4.

choices.text: A second DHCP server, handing out a gateway that points at itself
choices.why: Machines take the first offer; a home router in an office wall answers some of them first.

choices.text: The office DHCP pool has run out of addresses
choices.why: Machines left without an address would show 169.254, not a correct-looking configuration.

choices.text: A duplicate MAC address on two network cards
choices.why: That would trouble two machines, not half the building.

choices.text: The provider's line dropping in and out, so different machines catch it at different moments
choices.why: A flapping line affects every machine alike; the split here is per machine and it holds.

prompt: A department's printers and PCs are put on their own `/27` subnet. How many usable host addresses does that subnet have?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 4.

prompt: A client pointed its nameservers at a new DNS provider to move the website. The site works, and since the next morning nobody at the company receives mail. What is the likely cause?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

choices.text: The mailboxes are waiting for the change to propagate
choices.why: Nothing propagates; a day later the resolvers already see the new provider's records.

choices.text: The MX records stayed with the old provider and were never copied across
choices.why: Changing NS moves every record at once, including those that are missing in the new account.

choices.text: A CNAME at the bare domain is hiding the mail records
choices.why: A bare domain cannot carry a CNAME, and nothing says one was created.

choices.text: The new provider has blocked port 53
choices.why: Then the website would not resolve either.

prompt: You changed a site's `A` record an hour ago. A customer still reaches the old server. `dig @ns1.dnsprovider.net www.example.com` returns the new address; the customer's resolver returns the old one. What now?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

choices.text: Wait: the published answer is right, and that resolver keeps its copy until the TTL runs out
choices.why: The authoritative answer is what you published; an old copy elsewhere is a timer, not a fault.

choices.text: Edit the record again, since the resolver shows it was saved wrong
choices.why: The authoritative server already answers correctly; editing again restarts nothing useful.

choices.text: Lower the TTL now so the customer sees it at once
choices.why: A new TTL only reaches resolvers after their old copy expires.

choices.text: Move the domain's nameservers to a faster DNS provider
choices.why: That is the slowest change there is, and nothing is wrong with the published record.

prompt: A client's site fails with `SERVFAIL` for users on one public resolver and loads fine for users on another, with no pattern by city. What does the lesson point at?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

choices.text: The TTL still running out, resolver by resolver, after a recent change of address
choices.why: An expiring TTL serves an old address, not a failure.

choices.text: A typo in the name, which returns nothing
choices.why: A name that does not exist is NXDOMAIN, and it fails for everybody.

choices.text: The web server is overloaded
choices.why: SERVFAIL comes from the name lookup, before any web server is reached.

choices.text: DNSSEC signatures gone wrong
choices.why: A validating resolver refuses the bad signatures and a non-validating one answers happily.

prompt: A lookup can come back four ways. Match each to what it means.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 8.

pairs.left: `NXDOMAIN`
`NOERROR` with nothing in it
pairs.right: the name exists, with no record of that type

pairs.left: `SERVFAIL`
pairs.right: something broke on the way to the answer

pairs.left: a timeout
pairs.right: nothing answered, usually your own resolver's side

right_distractors: the record is cached and old

prompt: An internal app sits behind a reverse proxy. Users get `504 Gateway Timeout`. Where do you look first?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: At the users' browsers, since a 5xx is often a client sending a malformed request
choices.why: A malformed request is a 4xx; the 5xx family says the server side broke.

choices.text: At the proxy's own configuration, which rejected the request
choices.why: A proxy that rejected it would answer 4xx; a timeout says it waited on something behind.

choices.text: At the certificate, which has expired
choices.why: An expired certificate stops the browser before any status code arrives.

choices.text: At the application behind the proxy, which never answered it
choices.why: 504 is a proxy saying the thing behind it did not answer at all.

prompt: A permanent redirect is remembered by browsers, so a wrong one keeps sending visitors to the broken address after you fix it. The lesson's rule: publish a new redirect as a ___ first, and make it permanent once you are sure.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 6.

prompt: After a second web server was added behind the load balancer, users complain they are signed out at random, mid-task. What is the likely cause?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: The session cookie lacks `HttpOnly`, so scripts on the new server can read it and discard it
choices.why: HttpOnly hides a cookie from page scripts; it has nothing to do with which server answers.

choices.text: The idle timeout was set too short when the new server was installed
choices.why: An idle timeout ends sessions after inactivity, not in the middle of a task.

choices.text: The session table lives in each server's memory
choices.why: Half the requests reach a machine that has never heard of that session; a shared store fixes it.

choices.text: The session IDs are sequential and collide
choices.why: Guessable IDs are a security defect, and they do not sign people out.

prompt: A customer calls: on the shop's "My orders" page she sees another person's name and order history. The page went behind a CDN last week. Which header do you suspect first?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: `Cache-Control: no-cache`, which stops the CDN from checking
choices.why: no-cache means ask every time before using the copy.

choices.text: A session cookie with `SameSite=Lax`, which lets the CDN attach it to another visitor
choices.why: SameSite is about which site caused a request, not about shared caches.

choices.text: An `ETag` that is shared between customers
choices.why: An ETag only lets a cache ask whether its copy changed.

choices.text: `Cache-Control: public` on a response meant for one user
choices.why: Public lets the shared cache keep one visitor's page and serve it to the next.

prompt: A colleague used *copy as curl* on a failing request and wants to paste the command into the team's shared ticket. What is the problem?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 11.

choices.text: It carries the session cookie, which is a working login in plain text
choices.why: Anyone reading the ticket could replay the request as that user.

choices.text: It will not reproduce the fault, since the copied command runs without the page
choices.why: Running without the page is the point: it separates the browser from the server.

choices.text: It loses the headers, so the server will answer differently
choices.why: The copy carries every header and cookie; that is why it reproduces the request.

choices.text: The ticket system will run it by itself
choices.why: No.

prompt: A user says a form shows "Saved" and the change is not there. Put the diagnosis in the order the lesson walks it.
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 11.
items: Look at the console: no errors
Open the network panel, then submit the form again
Find the save request: its status is 200
Open its response body, which says validation failed
trap: Submitting before the panel is open records nothing, because the panel only records while it is open.

prompt: You are reviewing the `Set-Cookie` header for the cookie that says who a user is. Which attributes does the lesson want on it?
hint: Web and Internet Fundamentals, lesson 7.

choices.text: `Secure`
choices.why: It is never sent over plain HTTP.

choices.text: `HttpOnly`
choices.why: Scripts on the page cannot read it.

choices.text: `SameSite=Lax`
choices.why: Background requests from other sites do not carry it.

choices.text: `Domain=` set to the parent domain
choices.why: That widens it to every subdomain, including the least careful one.

choices.text: `SameSite=None`
choices.why: That is the old behaviour, for flows that leave and return; not the default for a login.

prompt: You ran `sudo usermod -aG deploy bruno`. `getent group deploy` lists him, yet in his open terminal he is still refused on the group's files. What do you tell him?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4.

choices.text: Log out and back in
choices.why: Group membership is attached to a process when it starts; his shell carries the old list.

choices.text: Run `sudo usermod -G deploy bruno` again, without the `-a` this time
choices.why: Without `-a` it replaces every other group he had, and his shell still would not see it.

choices.text: Give the files mode 777 so the group no longer matters
choices.why: It opens the files to everybody to work around a login that has not been refreshed.

choices.text: Wait for the change to reach `/etc/group`
choices.why: It is already there; getent just read it.

prompt: `report.txt` is `-rw-r--r--`, yet another user gets `Permission denied` reading it at `/srv/finance/q3/report.txt`. What does the lesson tell you to check?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4.

choices.text: Each directory on the way, with `namei -l` on the full path
choices.why: Every directory on the way needs `x`; one missing bit makes the file unreachable.

choices.text: The execute bit on the file itself, which reading a text file needs
choices.why: Reading a file needs `r`; `x` on a file is for running it.

choices.text: The umask of the user who created the file
choices.why: The umask shaped the mode at creation, and the mode already allows reading.

choices.text: Whether the other user is in the file's group, since the last three bits apply to the group
choices.why: The last three bits are for everybody else, and they allow reading.

prompt: A colleague ran `chmod -R 644 /srv/site` to "fix permissions". Now nobody can enter any directory in it. Which command repairs it without making every file executable?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4.

choices.text: `chmod -R u+rwX,go+rX /srv/site`
choices.why: Capital `X` gives execute to directories and to files that already had it.

choices.text: `chmod -R 755 /srv/site`
choices.why: It restores the directories and makes every text file executable too.

choices.text: `chmod -R u+rwx,go+rx /srv/site`
choices.why: Lowercase `x` is applied to files and directories alike.

choices.text: `chown -R www-data /srv/site`
choices.why: Ownership was never the problem; the directories lost their `x`.

prompt: `sudo echo 'nameserver 1.1.1.1' > /etc/resolv.conf` answers `bash: /etc/resolv.conf: Permission denied`. Why, and what works?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4.

choices.text: `echo` is a built-in that sudo cannot raise; use `/bin/echo`
choices.why: The message comes from bash, before sudo or echo were reached.

choices.text: The sudo password timed out; run `sudo -k` first
choices.why: An expired timestamp asks for the password again; `-k` ends it on purpose.

choices.text: `secure_path` hides `echo`
choices.why: That would be `command not found`, and it would come from sudo.

choices.text: Your own shell opens the file before sudo runs; pipe into `sudo tee` instead
choices.why: The redirect is the shell's work, and the shell is still you; `tee` under sudo opens the file as root.

prompt: To add bruno to `team` and keep every group he already has, the command is `sudo usermod ___ team bruno`.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4.

prompt: The file server was reinstalled last night. Today `ssh` to it prints `WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!`. What is the right move?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: Delete `~/.ssh/known_hosts` so the warning goes away for every server
choices.why: It throws away the check for every other host along with this one.

choices.text: Confirm the rebuild explains it, then `ssh-keygen -R` that host
choices.why: A rebuild is the likeliest of three causes; removing the stored key makes ssh ask again.

choices.text: Switch to password login, since the user's key is what changed on the server
choices.why: The warning is about the server's own key, not the one you log in with.

choices.text: Answer `yes`, as on the first connection
choices.why: It does not offer that; and a changed key is not to be cleared without knowing why.

prompt: `systemctl status` shows a red dot. Put the lines in the order the lesson reads them.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.
items: `Loaded:`, to see whether the unit was found at all
`Active: failed (Result: …)`, for how it failed
`Process: … status=…`, for the exit status
The journal lines at the bottom, for what the program said
trap: Going straight to the journal lines misses a `not-found` on the first line, which makes the rest beside the point.

prompt: A server rebooted overnight and nobody knows why. `journalctl -b ___` reads the log of the boot before the current one.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

prompt: An ordinary user runs `journalctl -u nginx` and sees nothing, though nginx logs plenty. Which of these would let them see the entries?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5.

choices.text: Running the same command with `sudo`
choices.why: An empty result as an ordinary user is usually permission, not absence.

choices.text: Membership of `systemd-journal`
choices.why: That group gives full read access to the journal.

choices.text: On Ubuntu, membership of `adm`
choices.why: On Debian and Ubuntu it does the same.

choices.text: Creating `/var/log/journal`
choices.why: That makes the journal survive a reboot; it changes nobody's access.

choices.text: Adding `-b` to the command
choices.why: It narrows to this boot, and the user still sees only their own messages.

prompt: A mail server says `No space left on device`, while `df -h` shows the filesystem 1% used. The other half of the question is `df ___`.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

prompt: A report job that ran for weeks is now found dead with exit status `137` and no log line of its own. Where does the lesson look first?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

choices.text: At the job's own log directory, for the exception it raised before it exited
choices.why: A killed process gets no chance to raise anything.

choices.text: At the job's permissions, since a denied file gives 137
choices.why: A permission failure to run is 126; 137 is a signal.

choices.text: At memory: `dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'`
choices.why: 137 is 128 + 9, a KILL from outside, and the OOM killer leaves its report in the kernel log.

choices.text: At the disk, for `I/O error` lines
choices.why: A failing disk leaves processes stuck in D, not killed with 137.

prompt: A monitoring alert fires because `free` on a 32 GB server shows 200 MB free and 30 GB in `buff/cache`. Which column does the lesson read before calling it a memory problem?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

choices.text: `available`
choices.why: It counts what a new program could get, including cache the kernel hands back.

choices.text: `shared`, which is where the cache is double-counted
choices.why: `shared` is tmpfs and shared segments, counted inside `used`.

choices.text: `free`, after dropping caches with `echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches`
choices.why: Dropping caches makes the machine slower and fixes nothing.

choices.text: `total`, compared with what was bought
choices.why: Total is what the kernel can see, and says nothing about pressure.

prompt: A backup process has sat in state `D` for twenty minutes, and `kill -9` as root changes nothing. What is the likely story?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6.

choices.text: It is a zombie, and its parent has to be killed
choices.why: A zombie shows `Z`; `D` is a process still inside the kernel.

choices.text: It was stopped with Ctrl+Z and is waiting for `fg`
choices.why: That is state `T`.

choices.text: It is waiting inside a kernel call on I/O, such as a network filesystem whose server has gone quiet

choices.why: Years of a tool on a junior advert describe the ideal, not the person hired.

choices.text: Windows, because the tasks described use it too
choices.why: Right. The day-one needs are often the ones the work mentions as well.

choices.text: The ITIL certificate, since it can be checked
choices.why: A certification usually sits on the would-like list.

choices.text: Python, since scripting pays off in any support role
choices.why: Nothing in the work mentions it; it is a nice-to-have here.

prompt: An advert for a junior role says you would be the one person responsible for the company's whole infrastructure. What does lesson 1 make of it?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 1.

choices.text: A good sign: you would learn everything at once
choices.why: With nobody to learn from, there is nobody to ask.

choices.text: A normal junior advert that lists the ideal, as they do
choices.why: The ideal lives in the requirements; being alone with everything is the job itself.

choices.text: A reason to wait until you have three years' experience
choices.why: The lesson's advice is to ask in the screening call, not to count years.

choices.text: A senior role at a junior salary; ask who you would learn from
choices.why: Right. Worth raising in the screening call.

prompt: Two offers: the service desk of a hospital's IT department, with an experienced lead who reviews your tickets; or a freelance contract paying a little more, with nobody else technical. By lesson 2, which is the stronger first job?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 2.

choices.text: The contract: pay decides a first job before anything else
choices.why: Pay comes third; a job that teaches raises the second salary more.

choices.text: The contract, since independence from day one is a sign of trust
choices.why: On a first job, independence from the start is a warning.

choices.text: The hospital: somebody more senior checks your work
choices.why: Right. Who will teach you comes before pay.

choices.text: Either, since both count as in-house IT
choices.why: A freelance contract is not in-house IT: nobody is there to teach you.

prompt: Which line describes an IT support lab project the way lesson 4 asks?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4.

choices.text: Documented and rebuilt a small-office network; a colleague rebuilt it from the runbook
choices.why: Right. What was done, what is true now, and how anybody could check.

choices.text: Used Windows Server, pfSense, Proxmox and PowerShell to build a complete office lab environment
choices.why: It lists what was used, not what now works or how to check it.

choices.text: Participated in setting up a lab network as part of a course
choices.why: Participated hides what you did; say which part.

choices.text: Responsible for the design, installation and support of a network
choices.why: Responsible for hides the result, and nothing in it can be checked.

prompt: Before a number goes on a CV line, which questions should you be able to answer? Choose all that apply.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4.

choices.text: Measured how?
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Compared with what?
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Whose was it, yours or the team's?
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Is it large enough to impress?
choices.why: A small true number beats a large one you cannot explain.

choices.text: Will a recruiter's search find it?
choices.why: Searches match words; a number is there to be checked.

prompt: At the end of your interview on the 14th they said they would decide by the 20th, and you sent a thank-you the next day. It is now the 17th. What does lesson 10 say?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 10.

choices.text: Send a short follow-up, a week being the usual gap
choices.why: The week is for applications; after an interview you wait for the date.

choices.text: Ask the recruiter for the status of the process
choices.why: They may not know or be allowed to say, and they gave you a date.

choices.text: Send nothing more until the 20th has passed
choices.why: Right. After an interview, you wait for the date they gave.

choices.text: Call the hiring manager's mobile to show interest
choices.why: A first contact through a door they did not open reads badly.

prompt: In a live exercise, the interviewer says a lab machine reaches the intranet but not the internet. You have repeated the problem back. What does lesson 12 do next?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 12.

choices.text: Restart the network service and see whether it clears
choices.why: That changes something before there is a plan, and the result would mean little.

choices.text: Say the plan and start editing the DNS settings
choices.why: The step after repeating it back is one question; the plan comes after.

choices.text: Ask whether it happens to everybody or to one machine
choices.why: Right. One question about what is unclear, then the plan, aloud.

choices.text: Work quietly, so as not to distract the interviewer
choices.why: Silence looks the same as having no idea.

prompt: An answer to "tell me about a time you worked under pressure". Match each sentence to its part of STAR.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 15.

pairs.left: On the first day of term, at a school's IT desk.
Thirty teachers' accounts had to work before the 07:30 lesson.
I reset them in timetable order and wrote each step down.
All worked by 07:20, and the steps became a runbook page.

prompt: In a screening call you are asked what you earn now, in a job at a shop. By lesson 17, how do you answer?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 17.

choices.text: With the shop salary, so the offer starts from it
choices.why: It says nothing about what this work is worth.

choices.text: With a figure a little above the shop's, to leave room
choices.why: That is still the shop's number, adjusted.

choices.text: With what you are looking for in this role
choices.why: Right. Pay from another field says nothing about this work.

choices.text: With a range, leaving out the kind of contract
choices.why: A range with no contract is ambiguous, rarely in your favour.

prompt: A CLT offer pays R$ 2,500 a month. With lesson 17's arithmetic (the 13th salary, the extra third on the holiday month, and FGTS at 8%), what PJ invoice, billed 12 months a year, matches the CLT year before tax? Answer in reais.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 17.

prompt: A junior offer's contract bars you from working for any IT company for two years after leaving, with no pay for that time. What does lesson 18 say?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 18.

choices.text: Sign it: such clauses are standard and never enforced
choices.why: The lesson reads it before signing and asks about it.

choices.text: Get a lawyer to review the whole contract before you answer the company at all
choices.why: A standard junior offer needs reading and one polite question per unclear point.

choices.text: Ask what it covers and whether it is paid, then question it
choices.why: Right. A broad, unpaid one on a junior contract is worth questioning.

choices.text: Turn the offer down, since the clause makes it illegal
choices.why: Nothing says it is illegal; it is something to ask about.

prompt: Your change to a login script this morning seems to have broken sign-in on the second floor. You think you could fix it alone within the hour. What does lesson 20 say?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20.

choices.text: Fix it quietly first, and report it once it is working
choices.why: An hour of silence fixing it alone turns a small mistake into an incident.

choices.text: Roll it back without a word, since no one has noticed yet
choices.why: What teams do not forgive easily is finding out later that you knew.

choices.text: Tell whoever needs to know now, then help fix it
choices.why: Right. Say it early; then fix it, or make way for who can.

choices.text: Write the team a long apology before doing anything
choices.why: A long apology makes somebody reassure you instead of fixing it.

prompt: At your first job you always restart the print spooler first, because you were told to. What does lesson 22 suggest doing with that habit?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 22.

choices.text: Keep doing it; the job will teach what it needs
choices.why: The work asks you to make it work, not to understand why.

choices.text: Drop it, since a restart is a guess
choices.why: The habit may be sound; the point is to learn why it is.

choices.text: Find out why it works
choices.why: Right. Ask why, once a week: that is how the fundamentals grow.

choices.text: Script it, so nobody has to think about it again
choices.why: Automating it teaches nothing about why it works.

prompt: Put lesson 8's ten-minute routine for aiming one application in order.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 8.
items: Read the advert for its three lists
Change the line under your name to the advert's words
Choose the five or six skills that match the day-one needs
Check that the top of the CV answers the two questions
Save and export it, apply, and add the row to the tracker
trap: Choosing skills before reading the advert picks them from habit, not from what this company needs on day one.
